steps.text: Solving equations is the core skill every university subject takes for granted – from physics to economics. For each type of equation there is a matching method. Recognise the types and you can solve almost anything.
steps.explanation:
Our roadmap:
1. Equivalence transformations and linear equations
2. Quadratic equations: the p-q formula and the quadratic formula
3. Zero-product rule and substitution
4. Rational and radical equations – with a check!
5. Exponential and logarithmic equations
steps.insight: Solving an equation means finding ALL numbers that satisfy it. The result is a solution set \(L\) – it can be empty, or contain one, several or infinitely many numbers.

steps.text: An equation is like a balance in equilibrium. As long as you do the same on BOTH sides, it stays balanced – and the solution set does not change.
steps.explanation:
Permitted equivalence transformations:
• Add or subtract the same number (or term) on both sides.
• Multiply or divide both sides by the same number \(\neq 0\).

The animation shows this with a balance: whatever is removed on the left must also go on the right.

The notation "\(| -2\)" on the right documents each step – often required at university.
steps.insight: Check: \(3 \cdot 4 + 2 = 14\) ✓. Optional for linear equations, mandatory for rational and radical equations.

steps.text: Linear equations (\(x\) only to the first power) are always solved the same way: remove brackets, all \(x\)-terms to one side, numbers to the other, divide by the coefficient.
steps.explanation:
Special cases at the end:
• \(0 \cdot x = 5\) – no number satisfies this: \(L = \emptyset\). Example: \(2x + 1 = 2x + 6\).
• \(0 \cdot x = 0\) – every number satisfies this: \(L = \mathbb{R}\). Example: \(2(x + 1) = 2x + 2\).

With fractions it helps to multiply by the common denominator first:
\(\frac{x}{2} + \frac{x}{3} = 10 \;\big|\cdot 6\;\) gives \(3x + 2x = 60\), so \(x = 12\).
steps.insight: A linear equation has exactly one, no or infinitely many solutions – never exactly two.

steps.text: One manipulation is dangerous and among the most common mistakes of all: dividing by a term containing the variable.
steps.explanation:
Dividing by \(x\) requires \(x \neq 0\). The case \(x = 0\) is silently excluded – and \(x = 0\) IS a solution: \(0^2 = 3 \cdot 0\).

Correct: bring everything to one side and factor out:
\(x^2 - 3x = 0 \iff x(x - 3) = 0 \iff x = 0 \text{ or } x = 3\).
steps.insight: Never divide by a term that might be \(0\). Instead, bring everything to one side and factorise.

steps.text: Before reaching for the big formula: many quadratic equations are solved faster directly.
steps.explanation:
• No \(x\)-term (only \(x^2\) and a number): solve for \(x^2\), take the root, don't forget \(\pm\)!
• No constant: factor out and use the zero-product rule.
• A square is never negative: \(x^2 = -4\) has no real solution.
steps.insight: \(x^2 = 49\) gives \(x = \pm 7\), not just \(x = 7\). The "\(\pm\)" is the most frequently forgotten part of solving quadratic equations.

steps.text: For the general form there are two equivalent formulas. The p-q formula for the normalised form (coefficient \(1\) in front of \(x^2\)):
steps.explanation:
Example: \(x^2 - 6x + 8 = 0\), so \(p = -6\), \(q = 8\):
\(x_{1,2} = 3 \pm \sqrt{9 - 8} = 3 \pm 1\), so \(x_1 = 4\), \(x_2 = 2\).

Careful with signs: \(-\frac{p}{2}\) with \(p = -6\) is \(+3\).

If there is a coefficient \(a \neq 1\) in front of \(x^2\), first divide the whole equation by \(a\). The formula is nothing but completing the square from "Terms & Manipulation", done in general.
steps.insight: Check by substituting or with Vieta's formulas: \(x_1 + x_2 = -p\) and \(x_1 \cdot x_2 = q\). Here: \(4 + 2 = 6\) ✓, \(4 \cdot 2 = 8\) ✓.

steps.text: The quadratic formula applies directly to \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\) with \(a \neq 0\):
steps.explanation:
Example: \(2x^2 + 3x - 2 = 0\), so \(a = 2\), \(b = 3\), \(c = -2\):
\(x_{1,2} = \frac{-3 \pm \sqrt{9 + 16}}{4} = \frac{-3 \pm 5}{4}\), so \(x_1 = \frac{1}{2}\), \(x_2 = -2\).

Which formula you use is a matter of taste. The quadratic formula saves dividing by \(a\); the p-q formula has fewer parts.

Common mistake: the \(2a\) in the denominator applies to the WHOLE numerator, not just the root.
steps.insight: If \(c < 0\) and \(a > 0\), then \(-4ac > 0\) – the discriminant is certainly positive and there are always two solutions.

steps.text: The expression under the root is called the discriminant \(D\). It decides the number of solutions – without solving the equation:
steps.formula: D = b^2 - 4ac \qquad \begin{cases} D > 0: & \text{two solutions} \\ D = 0: & \text{one solution } x = -\frac{b}{2a} \\ D < 0: & \text{no real solution} \end{cases}
steps.explanation:
Geometrically: the solutions are where the parabola \(y = ax^2 + bx + c\) crosses the \(x\)-axis. The animation shifts a parabola upwards: first it crosses the axis twice, then it touches it, then it floats above it.

Examples:
• \(x^2 - x - 6 = 0\): \(D = 1 + 24 = 25 > 0\) → two solutions (\(3\) and \(-2\)).
• \(x^2 + 4x + 4 = 0\): \(D = 16 - 16 = 0\) → one solution (\(-2\)).
• \(x^2 + 2x + 5 = 0\): \(D = 4 - 20 < 0\) → no real solution.
steps.insight: For \(D < 0\) there are two complex solutions – more on that in the topic "Complex Numbers".

steps.text: The zero-product rule is the most powerful tool for equations of higher degree:
steps.explanation:
A product is \(0\) exactly when (at least) one factor is \(0\). That's why factorising is so valuable when solving equations:

\((x - 2)(x + 5)(2x - 1) = 0\) \(\iff x = 2\) or \(x = -5\) or \(x = \frac{1}{2}\).

\(x^3 - 4x = 0\) \(\iff x(x^2 - 4) = 0\) \(\iff x(x - 2)(x + 2) = 0\), so \(L = \{-2, 0, 2\}\).

Careful: this ONLY works with \(0\) on the right-hand side. From \((x - 1)(x - 2) = 6\) it does NOT follow that \(x - 1 = 6\) or \(x - 2 = 6\).
steps.insight: First get \(0\) on one side, then factorise, then set each factor \(= 0\) separately.

steps.text: For equations like \(x^4 - 5x^2 + 4 = 0\), substitution helps: replace a recurring expression by a new variable.
steps.explanation:
Three steps:
1. Substitute: \(z = x^2\) turns the degree-four equation into a quadratic one.
2. Solve for \(z\) (p-q formula or factorising: \((z - 1)(z - 4) = 0\)).
3. Substitute back: each \(z\)-solution gives \(x\)-solutions. Negative \(z\) give no real solution for \(z = x^2\).

Substitution works whenever an expression and its square appear: \(e^{2x} = (e^x)^2\), \(x = (\sqrt{x})^2\), …
steps.insight: Don't forget to substitute back! The solutions for \(z\) are not yet the solutions of the original equation.

steps.text: Rational equations have the variable in a denominator. Procedure: determine the domain, multiply by the common denominator, solve, check against the domain.
steps.explanation:
Domain: \(x \neq 1\) and \(x \neq -1\).

Solve: \(3x + 3 = 2x - 2 \Rightarrow x = -5\). It lies in the domain, so \(L = \{-5\}\).

Why the check? Multiplying by the common denominator is only an equivalence transformation for \(x \neq \pm 1\). Extraneous solutions can appear – values that satisfy the new equation but are forbidden in the old one:

\(\frac{x}{x - 2} + 1 = \frac{2}{x - 2}\) gives \(x + (x - 2) = 2\) after multiplying, so \(x = 2\). But \(2 \notin D\), so \(L = \emptyset\).
steps.insight: With rational equations, the domain belongs at the start and the comparison with it at the end. Without that, the solution is incomplete.

steps.text: Radical equations are solved by squaring. But: squaring is NOT an equivalence transformation. \(a = b\) implies \(a^2 = b^2\), but not the other way round (\((-3)^2 = 3^2\)).
steps.explanation:
Candidates: \(x = 1\) and \(x = 6\). A check is mandatory:
• \(x = 1\): \(\sqrt{4} = 2\), but \(1 - 3 = -2\). ✗ Extraneous!
• \(x = 6\): \(\sqrt{9} = 3\) and \(6 - 3 = 3\) ✓

So \(L = \{6\}\). The extraneous solution \(x = 1\) solves \(-\sqrt{x + 3} = x - 3\) – squaring loses the sign.

Tip: isolate the root on one side before squaring. Otherwise squaring creates a mixed term with a root.
steps.insight: Squaring can add solutions but never remove any. So you find all solutions – but must sort out the false ones with a check.

steps.text: If the variable is in the exponent, the logarithm helps (see "Powers, Roots & Logarithms"). Two cases:
steps.explanation:
• Same base possible: write both sides as powers of the same base and compare exponents.
• Otherwise: isolate the power, then take logarithms. For base \(e\) use \(\ln\); in general \(a^x = b \iff x = \frac{\ln b}{\ln a}\).

Important: isolate the power first! In \(3 \cdot e^{2x} = 12\), divide by \(3\) first. \(\ln(3 e^{2x})\) would be \(\ln 3 + 2x\) – correct, but clumsy.

And: \(e^x = -2\) has no solution, because \(e^x > 0\) for all \(x\).
steps.insight: Exponential equations with \(e^{2x}\) and \(e^x\) are solved by substituting \(z = e^x\): \(e^{2x} - 3e^x + 2 = 0\) becomes \(z^2 - 3z + 2 = 0\).

steps.text: Logarithmic equations are solved the other way round: combine the logarithms, then exponentiate. The domain is especially important here – logarithms exist only for positive numbers.
steps.explanation:
Candidates \(x = -3\) and \(x = 2\). Compare with \(D\): \(-3 \notin D\). So \(L = \{2\}\).

Check: \(\ln 2 + \ln 3 = \ln 6\) ✓.

Why the extraneous solution? Combining \(\ln x + \ln(x + 1) = \ln(x(x + 1))\) enlarges the domain: \(x(x + 1) > 0\) also holds for \(x < -1\), where the individual logarithms are not defined.
steps.insight: Rule of thumb for rational, radical and logarithmic equations: domain at the start, check at the end.

steps.text: Look back at what you can do now:
steps.explanation:
1. Equivalence transformations on both sides. Never divide by a term that might be \(0\).

2. Quadratic: special cases directly, otherwise \(x = -\frac{p}{2} \pm \sqrt{\frac{p^2}{4} - q}\) or \(x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\). The discriminant determines the number of solutions.

3. Zero-product rule: first \(0\) on one side, then factorise. Substitution for \(x^4\), \(x^2\) or \(e^{2x}\), \(e^x\).

4. Rational and radical equations: domain or check – sort out extraneous solutions.

5. Exponential: isolate the power, take logarithms. Logarithmic: combine, exponentiate, check \(D\).
steps.insight: Congratulations! You have completed the first five topics of the bridging course. Next up are inequalities & absolute values – case distinctions make things a little trickier there.
